articles.title: St Mary’s Church in Rochdale Hosts Women’s Breakfast and Holy Communion Service
articles.excerpt: St Mary’s Church in Rochdale is hosting a Women’s Breakfast and a Holy Communion service this weekend, welcoming all to participate in community activities and fellowship.
articles.content_html:
St Mary’s Church in Rochdale is preparing for a busy weekend with two significant events. The church will host a Women’s Breakfast on Saturday, September 26, from 9am to 10.30am, following a summer break. This gathering will feature breakfast butties, fellowship, and a short gospel talk focusing on the theme of the Ten Commandments, specifically discussing the commandment to ‘honour your mother and father’. All women are welcome to attend without prior registration.

In addition to the Women’s Breakfast, St Mary’s will hold its regular Holy Communion service on Sunday, September 27, starting at 10.30am. The sermon will explore Matthew chapter 8, verse 18 to chapter 9, verse 8. Children’s groups will be available for ages 4 to 11, allowing families to participate fully in the service. After the service, attendees are invited to enjoy cake and refreshments, providing an opportunity for socialising and community connection.

The church is currently undergoing some building work on its roof, with scaffolding visible around the premises. However, church officials have confirmed that services will continue as usual during this period. New attendees are encouraged to join and will be welcomed warmly, especially during the post-service brew time, which aims to help newcomers integrate into church life.

For young people, the church offers a group called Insight, formerly known as Youth Bible Study, which meets on Sunday afternoons at Christ Church in Chadderton. This group is designed for teens in Years 10 to 13 and focuses on exploring the Bible and fostering friendships among peers. Parents interested in registering their children can contact Rev Ben Wilkinson for more information.

articles.title: Rochdale vs Oldham Derby Attracts Over 6,000 Fans to Spotland
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale vs Oldham derby at Spotland saw 6,121 fans in attendance, including nearly 2,000 from Oldham, creating a lively atmosphere ahead of the match.
articles.content_html:
The League Two derby between Rochdale and Oldham Athletic took place at Spotland on Saturday, drawing a crowd of 6,121 fans, including approximately 2,000 travelling supporters from Oldham. The match, which kicked off at 12.30pm, was marked by a vibrant atmosphere reminiscent of larger Manchester derbies, despite the lower league status of the teams involved.

Ahead of the match, Rochdale town centre was bustling with football fans, with many arriving early to enjoy the local pubs. By 10.30am, the area was lively, with police vans deployed to separate the rival supporters, who were engaging in friendly banter from behind cordons. Fans from both sides were dressed in club colours, adding to the festive spirit of the day.

The rivalry between the two clubs, separated by just seven miles, has a long history, and this match was no exception. The excitement was palpable as fans prepared for the encounter, with many taking to social media to share their anticipation in the days leading up to the game.

As the match unfolded, the local community and football fans alike were treated to a spirited display of football, showcasing the passion that both clubs inspire in their supporters. The event not only highlighted the significance of local rivalries in football but also brought together fans from different backgrounds in a shared love for the sport.

articles.title: Peacocks Signs Long-Term Lease at Rochdale Riverside Amid 15.3% Footfall Increase
articles.excerpt: British clothing retailer Peacocks has signed a long-term lease for a unit at Rochdale Riverside, contributing to a 15.3% rise in footfall at the shopping destination.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Riverside has welcomed British clothing retailer Peacocks, which has signed a long-term lease for a 10,181 sq ft unit at the shopping centre. This new addition brings the occupancy of Rochdale Riverside to 92%.

The announcement follows a significant 15.3% year-on-year increase in footfall at Rochdale Riverside, with nearly 200,000 visitors recorded in July 2026 alone. This trend of increasing visitor numbers has been consistent throughout the year, indicating a growing interest in the retail destination since its opening in Spring 2020.

RivingtonHark, which has managed the centre on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council since 2023, highlighted the importance of Peacocks' arrival in enhancing the shopping and leisure experience at Rochdale Riverside. The centre, which spans 200,000 sq ft, is anchored by a 50,000 sq ft Marks & Spencer store and features a six-screen Real Cinema, along with other national retailers such as Next, H&M, Boots, and JD Sports.

Councillor Danny Meredith, cabinet member for regeneration and housing at Rochdale Borough Council, expressed optimism about the new store, stating that Peacocks will be a popular addition to the shopping centre, which continues to thrive and attract more visitors. The ongoing success of Rochdale Riverside reflects the effective collaboration between local authorities and retail operators to enhance the town centre's appeal.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Launches Public Access Portal for Planning Applications
articles.excerpt: Residents can now access information on current planning applications through Rochdale Council's new online portal, providing transparency and ease of tracking local developments.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has launched a public access portal that allows residents to view current planning applications and decisions. This initiative aims to enhance transparency in local development processes.

The portal, available at publicaccess.rochdale.gov.uk, enables users to track the progress of submitted applications and access relevant documents. It includes details on various projects, including residential, commercial, and environmental developments.

Residents can search for specific applications by application number or address, making it easier to understand how developments may affect their neighbourhoods.

For further inquiries, residents can contact the planning department directly through the information provided on the website.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the local verb “cruckle”: what it means, where it comes from and why Rochdalians still claim it as part of home speech.
articles.summary: A short guide to the local verb “cruckle”: what it means, where it comes from and why Rochdalians still claim it as part of home speech.
articles.body:
If you grew up in the borough you will probably recognise the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” In Rochdale usage, to “cruckle” commonly means to roll or twist an ankle — that awkward stumble you can often walk off but which still makes you wince.

That everyday meaning is part folk memory and part linguistic continuity. Contemporary perceptual-dialect research into Greater Manchester finds that local people list “cruckle” among the words they associate specifically with Rochdale speech. A 2024 study using a draw‑a‑map / keywords method recorded “cruckle” in respondents’ descriptions of the borough’s speech, alongside other locally salient items such as guinnel (ginnel) and the label “broad.” In short: people in and around Rochdale strongly perceive the word as a local marker of speech.

But “cruckle” is not a new coinage. Historical dialect lexicons record an older verb-form usually written crookle (with variant spellings) meaning “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble.” Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary (late 19th–early 20th century) collects this family of forms across northern and midland dialects, and comparative work across Scots and Scandinavian dialects shows cognate forms with similar senses (to crouch, huddle or walk with bent limbs). Those older senses naturally cover both bending and awkward stepping — so a modern Rochdale meaning “to go over on one’s ankle” fits comfortably into the long-standing semantic field.

Linguists point to two predictable processes that produce words like cruckle: a crook/krug root that evokes bending or hooking, and a frequentative/imitative suffix –le that forms verbs for short or repeated actions (crook → crookle). Related forms — cruggle, krukel, kruggle and others — appear in Scots and northern English records and still survive in dialect collections. The Dictionary of the Scots Language, for example, lists cruggle/cruckle forms meaning “to crouch” or “to bow down,” showing how the same root has produced overlapping meanings across neighbouring dialect areas.

So is cruckle unique to Rochdale? The answer depends on what you mean by “unique.” Historical records show the root and related forms across northern England and Scots dialects, so the basic word-family is regional rather than geographically exclusive. What feels distinctly “Rochdale,” however, is the combination of continued local use, local recognition, and folk‑linguistic pride: many Rochdalians treat the word as a hometown specialism and use it as an emblem of local speech even if similar forms once existed elsewhere.

Why do dialect researchers take an interest in small words like this? Because compact, localised vocabulary reveals both continuing speech practice (who still uses a form) and folk awareness (which words people think mark their place). Modern perceptual work — crowd-sourced keyword mapping, interviews and heatmaps — shows how tiny pieces of vocabulary can carry outsized cultural meaning, function as local identity markers, and help scholars trace the survival and spread of dialect features.

If you want a simple take-away: the Rochdale meaning — to roll or twist your ankle — matches what local speakers report today; the form belongs to an older northern dialect family recorded by historical lexicographers and in Scots material; and recent perceptual research shows that many people strongly associate the word with Rochdale.

If you don’t know the word, try it next time you take a tumble in a ginnel — you’ll probably get a nod of recognition from someone from round here.

Sources used: a recent perceptual‑dialect study of Greater Manchester (Journal of Linguistic Geography, 2024) showing “cruckle” listed among words associated with Rochdale; historical dialect evidence from Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary recording crookle/cruckle senses; and the Dictionary of the Scots Language (Scots National Dictionary) documenting cognate forms (cruggle/cruckle) and their meanings.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Approves Additional Roof Works at Touchstones
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has approved additional roof works at Touchstones to enhance the building's facilities and ensure its preservation.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has approved additional roof works at Touchstones, a cultural venue in Rochdale. This decision was made during a recent council meeting, focusing on improving the building's facilities and ensuring its long-term preservation.

The works are part of ongoing efforts to maintain Touchstones, which serves as a hub for arts and heritage. The council acknowledges the venue's importance in supporting local culture and community engagement.

Details regarding the timeline for the roof works and any potential impact on the venue's operations have not yet been disclosed. The council is expected to provide updates as the project progresses.

This decision highlights the council's commitment to investing in local cultural assets. Further information can be found on the Rochdale Borough Council's official website.

articles.title: Rochdale Libraries Partner with Charity to Provide Free School Uniforms
articles.excerpt: Libraries across Rochdale are collaborating with Uniform For All to offer families access to free pre-loved school uniforms and shoes, addressing the rising costs of school attire.
articles.content_html:
Libraries across Rochdale are teaming up with the local charity Uniform For All to provide families with access to thousands of free pre-loved school uniforms and shoes. This initiative comes as many households struggle with the increasing costs associated with school attire, making it difficult for some families to afford essential items for their children.

The partnership aims to meet the growing demand for affordable alternatives by allowing families to collect high-quality pre-loved items, including polo shirts, skirts, trousers, branded school blazers, coats, and pumps. However, the challenge remains for some families who may not have the means to travel long distances to collect these items. To address this, Rochdale’s library service is facilitating the collection of these uniforms, enabling families to pick them up at their nearest library, thereby reducing travel costs.

In addition to providing uniforms, library staff will be available to offer further support related to the cost of living, including access to free Wi-Fi and computer facilities, as well as information on other benefits linked to library membership. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation, expressed support for the initiative, highlighting its importance in helping families during challenging times.

This collaboration not only assists families in obtaining necessary school items but also fosters community support through local libraries. Residents are encouraged to visit their local library to take advantage of this service and to seek additional assistance as needed.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky 'Fairies’ Chapel' in Healey Dell is part geology and industrial history — and part long‑running local folklore; here’s what we can verify and what belongs to story.
articles.summary: The rocky 'Fairies’ Chapel' in Healey Dell is part geology and industrial history — and part long‑running local folklore; here’s what we can verify and what belongs to story.
articles.body:
If you’ve stood beneath the arches of Healey Dell viaduct and peered into the Thrutch — a narrow, water‑scoured cleft in the Spodden — you’ll understand why people once spoke of a tiny chapel for otherworldly folk. The spot called the Fairies’ Chapel is a named feature inside Healey Dell Nature Reserve, which is run as a visitor site with a heritage centre and tea rooms on Dell Road. The reserve’s public information and the borough’s park listings make clear that Healey Dell is first and foremost a place of wildlife, waterfalls and industrial archaeology. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The core, verifiable landscape fact is straightforward: the River Spodden has cut into the local sandstone to create caverns, ledges and a pulpit‑like alcove in the gorge that people have long compared to a small chapel. Victorian and later visitors described seats and a pulpit formed by eroded rock; an 1838 flood is recorded locally as having altered the feature. Those geological and historical descriptions are what explain the place‑name — not any documentary evidence of supernatural beings. Local heritage material presents the “chapel” as a reading of natural rock formations rather than as a constructed building. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/history/))

The charming stories that give Healey Dell its fairy reputation come from the county’s older folklore tradition, preserved in 19th‑century collections. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire contains the best‑known account of the Fairies’ Chapel: a romantic narrative of millers, an enchanted cleft called the Thrutch, a Fairy Queen and a small bearded figure (sometimes called the Healey Dwarf) who features in meetings at the chapel. Roby collected and retold local tales in a literary style; his book helped fix versions of the story in print, but it is a record of oral tradition and imaginative retelling rather than a primary archival report of events. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm))

Later nineteenth‑ and twentieth‑century guidebooks and local leaflets repeated and embellished Roby’s tales, mixing fairies with witches, prophecy and other colourful motifs. Modern interpretation at the Healey Dell Heritage Centre treats these stories explicitly as folklore for visitors — there is a place for storytelling, performances and a children’s “Fairy Grotto,” but the centre’s materials separate those tales from the documented history of mills, bridges and the disused Rochdale–Bacup railway. If you want to hear the legends, the heritage centre is where they are told; if you want to see the historical record, the viaduct, mill remains and council descriptions are the source. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/attractions/))

The viaduct that frames much of the Dell’s scenery is itself a protected historic structure: Healey Dell Viaduct is a Grade II listed Victorian railway viaduct, recorded on the National Heritage List for England and described in detail by Historic England (listing first entered 30 November 1984). That listing documents the industrial past that shaped the valley — the mills, tramways and railway infrastructure — and anchors the Dell’s public significance in tangible, dated engineering heritage rather than in folklore. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? As a matter of verifiable fact, there is no documentary evidence that supernatural beings have met in the Thrutch. The “Fairies’ Chapel” name and the stories attached to it are part of Lancashire’s long oral and printed folklore tradition, powerfully popularised in the nineteenth century and kept alive locally through guides, performances and family storytelling. Those tales are valuable — they tell us how people have looked at landscape and memory — but they belong to culture and imagination rather than to the official historical record. Visitors can enjoy both the rock‑cut chapel and the stories it inspired, remembering to keep the two kinds of truth — geological and folkloric — clearly apart.
